newsitem.title: USA: Latin American stocks enjoy New Year boom.
newsitem.headline: Latin American stocks enjoy New Year boom.

text.p: Investors seeking fresh stocks and stronger returns are driving a boom in Latin American stock markets, which could outpace record-setting Wall Street this year.
However, analysts warn that the renewed attention paid to Latin America could fade in the face of higher U.S. interest rates.
The boom has surprised some analysts and echoed on New York exchanges as well, where bellwether stocks from the region have seen heavy trade and some record highs.
"We are very optimistic. We are saying that 1997 will be the year of Latin American equities," said Vinod Sehgal, director of Latin American research at Oppenheimer & Co.

As of Thursday, Latin American stock markets have risen 8.5 percent since the start of the year, according to the Morgan Stanley Capital International index. The markets are topping even Asia, which has seen a 4.1 percent rise.

Leader among the skyrocketing exchanges is Colombia, which has soared 24.1 percent. It is trailed by regional heavyweights Mexico, up 9.8 percent, Argentina, up 7.8 percent, and Brazil, which has seen a 7.5 percent rise.
The only market not registering an advance is Venezuela, which has dropped 2.7 percent.
Mexico's leading IPC share index hit an intraday record on Thursday of 3,753.18 in very heavy trading, although it later fell on profit-taking to close at 3,701.83.
The rise followed the seventh record close of the year on Wednesday, helped by Mexico's announcement that it would pay $5 billion in international emergency loans ahead of schedule.
By comparison, the Dow Jones industrial average has risen 4.9 percent from the start of the year through Thursday, despite seven record closes.
Analysts said several factors were helping Latin American markets. They include:
-- solid economic fundamentals as the region puts its history of high inflation behind it, sells off state companies and lowers trade barriers;
-- predictions that Latin America's gross domestic product will grow from 4 to 4.5 percent this year, above the United States' likely growth of about 3 percent;
-- relatively low interest rates around the world;
-- the so-called "January effect" as portfolio managers rejig their investments at the start of the year;
-- and, especially, investors looking abroad for new higher-yielding stocks as the pace begins to slow on the U.S. markets' record runs and fixed-income investments lose their luster.
"We went into the new year with a lot of new money going into the region," said Geoffrey Dennis, global emerging markets strategist for HSBC James Capel in New York.
"We think this year we are going to have a dull U.S. market. Net-net, it is not going to go up very much."
He predicted Latin American markets would rise 22 percent in 1997, and Oppenheimer's Sehgal foresaw rises of 20 percent in Argentina and between 15 and 20 percent in Mexico.

January's rise marks another strong step back from the market slide after Mexico's fiscal crisis in December 1994. In dollar terms, markets in the region lost 2 percent in 1994, 18 percent in 1995 and then rose 16 percent last year, according to the World Bank's International Finance Corp.

In New York, the Latin American surge has included shares in such regional bellwethers as telecommunications companies Telefonos de Mexico, Brazil's Telebras, Telefonica del Peru and Argentine oil company YPF. All have been on the New York Stock Exchange's list of most-active stocks.

However, analysts warned that a similar boom last year fizzled when the Federal Reserve raised interest rates in the spring. A rate rise would cool off New York markets, drive money into U.S. Treasuries and other fixed-income funds and pull it out of Latin America.
"The only danger is an upside move" in U.S. rates, said HSBC James Capel's Dennis.
